profile.reading: This is one of three data center buildings on Vantage Data Centers' New Albany, Ohio campus at 3325 Horizon Court, in the New Albany International Business Park spanning Licking and Franklin counties, now one of the largest concentrations of hyperscale data center construction in the eastern United States. The park has drawn Amazon Web Services, Google, Meta, Microsoft, and Vantage, attracted by AEP Ohio's transmission capacity, Ohio's data center sales-and-use-tax exemption program, and local economic-development incentive agreements negotiated with New Albany and Licking County. Vantage's own campus materials describe the site as roughly 70 acres with about 1.5 million square feet planned across three two-story buildings, each stated at approximately 64 megawatts of critical IT capacity, for a total campus capacity near 192 megawatts once fully built out; Vantage's page does not assign individual names, building numbers, or separately confirmed square-footage figures to each of the three structures beyond this uniform per-building description, so an even division of the 1.5 million total (approximately 500,000 square feet per building) is this profile's derived estimate rather than an operator-confirmed figure for this specific building. Vantage has stated the first of the three buildings was slated to reach operational status in December 2025, with additional phases continuing through 2028, meaning this building, if it is the second or third phase, could still have been under construction as of this writing. Power is supplied end-to-end at 480 volts, with N+1 electrical and N+2 mechanical redundancy per Vantage's standard design approach, and each building is targeted for LEED Silver certification. Vantage Data Centers, headquartered in Denver, is backed by DigitalBridge and Silver Lake, which committed $6.4 billion in fresh capital to the company in January 2024. Ohio's rapid data center buildout, concentrated heavily in New Albany and neighboring Licking County communities, has become a subject of statewide debate over electricity rate impacts on residential ratepayers, prompting AEP Ohio to propose a distinct large-load tariff classification for data centers before the Public Utilities Commission of Ohio, and prompting New Albany-area school districts and township trustees to weigh the tradeoffs between data-center tax revenue and rising local electricity demand.

reading.body:
Vantage Building 3 is one of three identical data center structures planned for a 70-acre New Albany, Ohio campus, each designed for 64 megawatts of critical IT load, totaling 192 megawatts across the campus through 2028. The operator targeted the first building for December 2025, but actual operational status of this specific building is not confirmed as of this writing. At an industry-standard assumption of 40 kilowatts per rack in AI training density, a single 64 MW building represents roughly 1,600 racks of accelerator capacity, suggesting the full three-building campus is designed to host on the order of 4,800 racks once complete.

The campus qualifies for LEED Silver certification and is supplied with N+1 electrical and N+2 mechanical redundancy at 480 volts. New Albany sits in the largest concentration of hyperscale data center construction east of the Mississippi, alongside facilities from Amazon, Google, Meta, and Microsoft, drawn to AEP Ohio's transmission capacity and Ohio's data center tax exemptions. The rapid buildout has triggered a statewide rate debate, prompting AEP Ohio to propose a distinct tariff classification for large data center loads before Ohio's Public Utilities Commission.

This campus represents the only published megawatt figure in Ohio in this registry, making it the leading confirmed project in the state by disclosed capacity, though five other facilities are mapped in Ohio with no published specifications. The site's phased completion through 2028 means its full capacity will not contribute to grid demand simultaneously; the timing and sequencing of each building's actual operational debut remain to be verified as construction progresses.
